Dossier

Say it to your boss.

A big goal can feel exciting and scary at the same time. This dossier gives you the research, the sentences and the grammar to talk to your boss about it.

Tap or hover any highlighted phrase or dotted word to see it in Portuguese.

Talk about these first

Then read the article and see who agrees with you.

  1. Think of a goal that felt too big. Who gave it to you? What did you do?
    “My teacher wanted a presentation in English in two weeks. I was scared. I asked her for an example, and she showed me one. After that, it felt possible.”
  2. How do you usually receive a goal: in a meeting, by email or in a short message? Which one do you prefer?
    “I prefer a meeting. I can ask questions right away. A message is fast, but I do not know what my boss really wants.”
  3. When did you stay quiet, and you wish you had spoken? What was the fear?
    “In a meeting, my boss changed the deadline to Friday. I knew it was too short, but I said nothing. I was afraid he would think I was lazy.”
  4. What is one sentence you would like to say to your boss, but you never say?
    “I need more time.” I think I will say it next week.
  5. Can a boss make it easy for you to speak up? How?
    “Yes. My boss asks ‘What do you think?’ and then she waits. She does not answer for us.”
Work · Bosses

Four things to say to your boss

Four short sentences can make the talk with your boss easier. Here they are, with the research behind them.

By EIC Magazine · 3 min read · Hover over the dotted words to see them in Portuguese

Listen to the article0:00
Speed
The recording is not on this page yet.

A big goal can feel exciting and scary at the same time. Most people do not say how they feel. They nod, they say “OK,” and they worry alone.

In 1980, John Gabarro and John Kotter wrote “Managing Your Boss” for Harvard Business Review. Their main idea is simple: your relationship with your boss is part of your job, and you and your boss depend on each other. Here are four things you can say to make it better.

Ask for clarity

Do not guess what your boss wants. Gabarro and Kotter advise you to ask about priorities and expectations. A boss may say “do your best,” but you need more than that. Ask for a number, a date and an example. Try this: “What does success look like?”

Say it early

Bosses need to hear bad news early. Gabarro and Kotter say that a promise about an easy date can please your boss today and upset your boss later, if you do not keep it. One president in the article would rather have a steady employee than one with a few big successes. If a goal is in danger, say so today, not on the last day. Try this: “I see a risk.”

Disagree calmly

Why is it hard to disagree? Jim Detert and Amy Edmondson studied this and published their research in 2011. They found that many people follow unspoken rules in their heads. People use these rules to decide if speaking up is safe, and they do it without thinking. These rules can keep people quiet in the workplace. So start small. Say what you agree with first. Then give one fact and one option: “I agree with the goal. The date worries me. Could we move it by one week?”

Ask for what you need

A big goal needs time, people or information. Name what you need and say why: “I need this to do it well.” Gabarro and Kotter add a warning: your boss’s time is limited, so save your requests for the important things. The sentences to say are advice for this lesson, not research findings.

Before your next meeting, choose one sentence and say it out loud. The first time is the hardest. After that, it gets easier.

“I agree with the goal. The date worries me. Could we move it by one week?”A sentence for this lesson

1980the year Gabarro and Kotter published “Managing Your Boss” in Harvard Business Review
4 studiesin Detert and Edmondson’s 2011 research on why people stay quiet at work
5 kindsof unspoken rules about speaking up, measured in those studies
180 teamsstudied by Google: psychological safety came first of five dynamics

Sources: Gabarro and Kotter, Managing Your Boss, Harvard Business Review (1980; reprinted 2005); Detert and Edmondson, Implicit Voice Theories: Taken-for-Granted Rules of Self-Censorship at Work, Academy of Management Journal (2011); Google re:Work, Understand team effectiveness.

4Fears

Why we stay quiet

Why do people stay quiet? Detert and Edmondson found that people follow unspoken rules in their heads, and they follow them without thinking. Often nobody checks if the fear is true. The four fears below are common examples, written for this lesson.

Four fears

  1. My boss will be offended.
  2. It will hurt my career.
  3. I will look weak.
  4. I will be the only one.

Which fear is it?

0 / 0 correct

Read what each person thinks. Choose the fear behind the thought.

Example
Paulo thinks: “If I say no to this project, my boss will remember it when promotions come.”
It will hurt my career.

He is thinking about his future at the company. That is the fear for his career.

1
The goal is too big. Ana thinks: “If I say 600 is too much, my boss will take it as a criticism of him.”
2
The deadline is too short. Bruno thinks: “If I ask for more time, they may give the next big project to someone else.”
3
You need help. Carla thinks: “If I ask for help, everybody will see that I am not as good as the others.”
4
You need help too. Diego thinks: “Nobody else asks for help in this team. I do not want to be the first.”
5
You see a mistake in the plan. Elisa thinks: “She wrote this plan herself. If I say there is a problem, she will be upset.”
6
You disagree in a meeting. Fábio thinks: “If I disagree in front of everybody, my next review may be bad.”

Has this fear ever really happened to you? Many people never test their fear.

Your turn · your fear

Think of one time you did not say something to a boss, a teacher or a coach. Which fear was it? Did it really happen?

“I did not tell my teacher that the test date was a problem. I was afraid she would be upset. Later, I told her. She said: ‘Thank you, I did not know.’ The fear did not come true.”
5Chunks

Chunks and patterns

The four things to say use the same phrases again and again. Learn the whole phrase and the pattern that goes with it, and the sentence builds itself.

Three families you already know

Three of the sentences you will say use verb patterns. The first verb decides what comes next. These are the same Families 1, 2 and 3 from the Verb Patterns lesson.

FamilyThe patternThe verbsExample
1verb + person + to + verbask · need · want · would like · expect“I’d like you to explain the priority.”
2let · make · have + person + verbOnly three verbs. No to after the person.“Could you let me know if the plan changes?”
3suggest · recommend · propose + that + person + verbFormal. The verb stays in the base form: that we move, that she join.“I suggest that we move the date by one week.”

Where the not goes

FamilyWhere the not goesExample
1Two places“I didn’t ask them to start.” × “I asked them not to start.”
2The first verb“I didn’t let them start.” Never “I let them not start.”
3After that“I suggest that they not start.” Never “that they don’t start.”

8The case

Marina sets her goal

Marina works in customer support. Her boss wants a big goal for the next quarter. Look at her track record and her conditions, then choose a goal that she can defend. The numbers are invented for this lesson. They are not real data.

  1. 1Ask for clarity

    What does success look like? Is 600 the number for every month, or for the whole quarter?

    Ask before you guess.

  2. 2Say it early

    I see a risk: one person leaves in November, so we will be four, not five.

    Say it today, with a fact.

  3. 3Disagree calmly

    I agree with the goal. The number worries me. Could we start at 520?

    Agree first. Then give one fact and one option.

  4. 4Ask for what you need

    I need two weeks to learn the new tool. Could you let me know if it changes the plan?

    Name what you need, and say why.

Marina's track record

QuarterTickets per month
Last year, Q4410
Q1430
Q2450
Q3440

Her average is about 430 tickets a month.

Her conditions now

  • One person leaves in November. The team goes from five people to four.
  • A new tool arrives in December. It may help, but nobody knows how much yet, so the calculation does not count it.

Try three goals

With four people, Marina can keep her pace and do about 344 tickets a month (430 × 4 ÷ 5). The score is 344 divided by the goal. Google says 60 to 70 percent is the sweet spot for an ambitious goal. Try three goals: 600, 520 and 480. On your page, write the score for each one.

Your turn · the case

Choose a goal that you have now, at work or at school. Use the four things to talk to your boss, teacher or coach. Say it out loud, in under one minute.

“What does success look like? I see a risk: the exam is in the same week as my project. I agree with the goal. The date worries me. Could we move the project by one week? I need two extra classes to practice. Could you let me know if that is possible?”

10Glossary

Watch out, then look it up

False friends

WordFrom the PortugueseWhat it really means
realizerealizarIt means to notice or understand. For a goal, say reach or achieve. Say: We reached the goal.
assumeassumirIt means to suppose something is true. For responsibility, say take responsibility. Say: I take responsibility for the plan.
pretendpretenderIt means to fake something. For a plan, say intend to. Say: We intend to finish by Friday.
supportsuportarIt means to help. For something hard to bear, say handle or stand. Say: He cannot handle the pressure.
compromisecompromissoA compromise is an agreement in which each side gives something up. For a duty or a promise, say commitment.
